title: The thousandth lotus
hook: Vishnu, one lotus short, offers his own eye; why the flower on the shrine stands for the one who offers it
carry: the flower stands for your heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, deepa, the lamp. Your line was the lamp's light is greeted as god. Today, the thing on the plate that won't last the day, and a god who ran out of them.
screen: `DEEPA — THE LAMP'S LIGHT IS GREETED AS GOD.`

segments.voice: The gods were losing to the demons, and Vishnu went to Shiva's mountain to ask for help. He didn't come empty-handed. He brought a thousand lotuses, one for each of Shiva's thousand names, and began: a name, a flower. A name, a flower. Shiva watched, and decided to test him. Quietly, he hid one lotus. Nine hundred and ninety-nine names in, Vishnu reached into the basket, and it was empty. He didn't stop the prayer. He didn't send anyone to find another flower. People call Vishnu lotus-eyed. So he got ready to offer his own eye.
screen: `A THOUSAND NAMES, A THOUSAND LOTUSES.` → `SHIVA HIDES ONE.` → `THE BASKET IS EMPTY.` → `VISHNU OFFERS HIS OWN EYE.`

segments.voice: Shiva stopped him, deeply moved, and gave Vishnu the shining discus he carries ever since, the Sudarshana. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it. Look at what the story says a flower is. When the basket ran out, Vishnu didn't see a missing decoration. He saw a gap only he could fill, because the flower had been standing in for him the whole time. That's the heart of bhakti, devotion, the path of love: in puja, the flower is a stand-in for the one who offers it. Krishna says the same thing another way: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with love, and I accept it. The price doesn't matter. The heart does. So a shrine flower comes with small habits. It's picked fresh for the morning, and yesterday's is taken down. One that fell on the floor is usually not offered. It's often left unsmelled, because the first enjoyment isn't the giver's. Different forms of God have favorites: red hibiscus for Ganesha and the Goddess, bilva leaves for Shiva, tulsi for Vishnu and Krishna. And by evening it droops, so tomorrow you bring a new one, the way you bring yourself again. Many teachers read it simply: the flower on the plate is really you. So a silk flower can sit there all year, and it's pretty. It just can't stand in for anyone.
screen: `SHIVA GIVES THE SUDARSHANA.` · `BHAKTI: THE FLOWER STANDS FOR YOU.` · `PICKED FRESH, LEFT UNSMELLED.` · `A NEW ONE TOMORROW, LIKE YOU.`

segments.voice: Find a flower or a leaf near you, or picture one, and look at it closely: the color, the veins, the edge that won't look like this tomorrow. Set it down somewhere that matters to you, your corner, a windowsill, beside a photo of someone you love. If you pray, offer it with a name you honor, Om namah shivaya, or Krishna's name, and let it carry you with it. If you don't pray, name one thing you're bringing with it today, and sit with it.
Pushpa. The flower: picked fresh, left unsmelled, and offered in your place, the way Vishnu's lotuses were.
Your line: the flower stands for your heart. Vishnu was ready to give himself when the flowers ran out. That's day one hundred thirteen.

screen: `THE FLOWER STANDS FOR YOUR HEART.` → `DAY 113 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE NAME HE CALLED.`

howItsDone: Many Hindus place fresh flowers at the home shrine each morning as an offering of devotion (bhakti), taking down the previous day's, usually not offering a fallen flower or smelling one meant for the shrine, and often choosing flowers or leaves dear to a particular deity, such as hibiscus for Ganesha, bilva for Shiva and tulsi for Vishnu or Krishna.

what a scholar hears: pushpa is one of the standard upacharas, the services of puja; Gita 9.26 names leaf, flower, fruit and water as accepted when given with devotion; and the Shiva Purana tells of Vishnu receiving the Sudarshana after offering a thousand lotuses and, one short, his own eye.
